versions.short: The bill would require the Federal Protective Service, which guards federal buildings, to create and carry out guidance on how to alert federal workers in those buildings about law enforcement emergencies such as violent threats, weapons incidents, suspected terrorism, or suspicious devices, both inside the building and within about 150 feet of its outer edge. The guidance would also cover telling tenants how to stay safe during an immediate threat or a higher risk of one. Each building's designated security official would be responsible for putting this guidance into practice. The Service would also have to make sure federal tenants can respond adequately to such crises and test their preparedness periodically. Within one year, the Service would have to report to Congress on the practices adopted, in no more than 10 pages, and brief lawmakers on it. The bill states that no additional funds are authorized to carry it out.
